utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the Registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-87-PT, the Prosecutor versus Milan Milutinovic, Nikola Sainovic, Dragoljub Ojdanic, Nebojsa Pavkovic, Vladimir Lazarevic, Vlastimir Djordjevic, and Sreten Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And may we have the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm Tom Hannis, on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor. I'm here today as an interested observer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And for Canada?

utterances.speaker: MS. SWORDS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Colleen Swords. I appear on behalf of the Government of Canada, and I'm assisted today by Janet Henchey from my Department of Justice, John Currie from the Department of Foreign Affairs, and Masud Husain from our embassy here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. For the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. RAAB
utterances.text: Your Honours, my name is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RAAB
utterances.text: My name is Dominic Raab. I'm the legal advisor for the British embassy here in The Hague, and I'll be making the oral submissions on behalf of the Government of the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Raab, and nothing is to be read in the fact that you're all sitting where the accused usually sit. For the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm Clifton Johnson and I'm here for the United States and I'll assisted by Heather Schildge and Omar Nazif.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Tomislav Visnjic and Peter Robinson on behalf of the General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, as you all know, this is the second application by the accused Ojdanic pursuant to Rule 54 bis, and I'll ask his representatives to make their opening statement. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Good afternoon, Mr. President, members of the Trial Chamber. First of all, again I want to thank the States for their participation in these proceedings. I think we've been successful in narrowing our request, just judging by the number of States that are now parties to these proceedings, so I think we could say that we're fishing in a smaller pond today. I want to advise the Trial Chamber of what we did since your decision of 23 March 2005. We studied your decision in detail. We essentially extracted every sentence from that decision and concurring opinion which addressed deficiencies in our earlier request, diagrammed those sentences like I was taught in grammar school, and we sat down with General Ojdanic and attempted to comply in full with every single word of the decision and concurring opinion. Our reformulated request, first dealing with intercepted conversations of General Ojdanic in paragraph A and intercepted conversations mentioning General Ojdanic in paragraph B, we saw that the decision suggested that we stipulate as far as possible the place and the dates of the intercepted conversation, and so we did that. First with the place: General Ojdanic did spend a few days outside of Belgrade, but by and large for the entire period he was in Belgrade and so we were able to limit our request to conversations occurring while he was in Belgrade. With respect to the dates: Although General Ojdanic can recall some dates of some conversations of -- about Kosovo which are well documented, such as those with General Wesley Clark, his conversations with President Milosevic and with his subordinates during this period were on essentially a daily basis, and during the bombing of NATO, there was a frenzy of activity with many conversations, and so in speaking with him I found it was impossible to limit the request any narrower than the five-month period set forth in our original request, which is a period in which he had almost daily contact regarding Kosovo. So we were unable to narrow the request as to date, but we were able to make another narrowing, and that is as to participants. We came up with the alternative of narrowing the request by listing the other participant to the conversation. In discussing with General Ojdanic, I found that his conversations about Kosovo were by and large limited to a group of subordinates, and so we were able to list those people in Annex A and make our request more specific by limiting the intercepted conversations to those with 23 identified persons. Request B presented a different problem because it involves conversations in which General Ojdanic was not a party, and so we decided to limit our request to those conversations in which at least one party to the conversation held a position in the government, the armed forces, or the police in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or Serbia. By doing this, we thought that these people were more likely to have relevant, useful information about General Ojdanic's activities and state of mind relating to Kosovo and that we could reduce the burden on the States. Now, both the decision and separate opinion noted that we needed to specify the particular matters in issue in the case to which the documents sought were relevant and how they were relevant, so we did that. For intercepted conversations, we identified four central issues in the case: General Ojdanic's knowledge or participation or lack thereof in the intended or actual deportation of Albanians from Kosovo; his knowledge or participation in the intended or actual killing of civilians in Kosovo; whether the formal chain of command on matters pertaining to Kosovo was respected; and his efforts to prevent and punish war crimes in Kosovo. And so if a conversation falls within any of these four categories, it should be produced. I think this goes to the very core of the issues that will be at the trial of this case. We're not trying to write the history of the Balkans. We set forth how the documents were relevant to these issues. For example, that General Ojdanic contends he had no knowledge of any plan to expel Albanians nor did he participate in assisting or carrying out such a plan, and these intercepted conversations will go directly to that issue or else they won't have to be produced. And the same with the killings. And with respect to the chain of command, we noted that the Prosecution's own evidence in the Milosevic trial has indicated that the formal chain of command, which included General Ojdanic, may not have been respected in matters pertaining to Kosovo, and so these intercepted conversations will assist us in determining whether or not General Ojdanic had knowledge of or was a participant in any plan to expel Albanians from Kosovo. And likewise, with respect to failing to prevent and punish crimes, General Ojdanic contends that did he take steps to prevent and punish crimes in Kosovo, and we hope that the intercepted conversations would be -- provide us evidence which could assist us in proving that during the trial. So we feel that we did everything we could to fully comply with the decision and separate opinion with regard to the specificity and relevance and necessity of the intercepted conversations. And perhaps even we narrowed it too much because now States like the United Kingdom and Germany and France and Netherlands, which presumably had responsive information to our wider request say that they have nothing to give to us now that our request is this narrow. We also note that no state now contents that they have been unable to conduct a search of their records because of lack of specificity, and in fact Canada and the United States have acknowledged that they have been able to identify material responsive to these requests. The Trial Chamber in its decision quoted the Kordic Appeals Chamber decision that the underlying purpose of the requirement of specificity is to allow a State to be able to identify the requested documents. We believe that that purpose has been accomplished by our reformulated request. With respect to request C, the Trial Chamber was very critical of our request for records of statements by General Ojdanic to representatives of the States, including sources of information working on their behalf. The majority said that it was vague and obscure, and Judge Bonomy said it lacked basic clarity, so we decided to scrap our catch-all approach with respect to request number C and just ask for specific documents that we now know in 2005 are in existence and we have not been able to obtain from the Prosecution or in our own investigation. When we made the initial request back in 2002 we contemplated making subsequent requests once we'd had a chance to see the disclosure in the case and do our own investigation, but we decided now we would just simply include those things that we have now learned are relevant and that we need, and so there will be no subsequent requests, barring unforeseen developments, and we've included the three items that we are requesting under item C, and they're three very specific items. First, the information relating to General Ojdanic's speech to the foreign military attaches in Belgrade in July or August 1998. And we provided the relevance of that by citing to the testimony of John Crosland, the British attache in the Milosevic case, in which he gives an account of what General Ojdanic said, and we have explained in our application that General Ojdanic believes that Colonel Crosland has mischaracterised what he said, so we want to obtain what the other military attaches at the meeting reported about that speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is this a new request or is it the old request reformulated to respond to the concerns expressed?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a very good question. I would have to say it's a new request in the sense that it falls outside the time period of our original request. And should the Trial Chamber also deem this to be a new request, we would ask that you consider it in conjunction with the reformulated requests. I believe that we're not prohibited from making a new request at any time and it would expedite matters if we could have them considered at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, has General Ojdanic got the text of his speech?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what does it matter what anyone else thought of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, the text of his speech is something that's been in his possession and is subject to disputes as to credibility, so I think the more accurate information we could get from other sources, especially the belligerents from NATO, would enhance the credibility of perhaps the determination the Trial Chamber will have to make between General Ojdanic and Colonel Crosland at the end of the trial. Our second specific item in request number C is concerning the contacts between General Clark and General Ojdanic, and we have again indicated that specific pages of General Clark's book in which some evidence of those contacts could be found. And just to give you an idea of what we're talking about, in General Clark's book he talks about a meeting on page 156 with General Ojdanic in December of 1998, and he said that Sainovic, the civilian minister in charge of Serb activities, insisted on being present for the entire meeting. "I figured the Serbs didn't quite trust Ojdanic and probably -- especially not in a room with me." And he goes on to talk about how he made a statement to General Ojdanic about violating the agreements, and General Ojdanic listened and appeared confused. Sainovic spoke to him in Serbian and then he replied that it was permitted for our forces to be there. And again when General Clark responded, the confused appearance by Ojdanic was noted, with Sainovic offering more explanations. And General Clark concludes that: "I realised as the dialogue continued that I was talking to a place holder -" referring to General Ojdanic - "someone who was ambitious enough to want the job and maybe not smart enough to ask too many of the hard questions that had gotten General Perisic in trouble." And in another passage from the book, at page 165, he speaks of a phone conversation between General Ojdanic and himself in March of 1999, just on the eve of the NATO bombing, and he talks about how General Ojdanic said that he was moving the forces into Kosovo to defend themselves from NATO, not for any actions against the Albanians, and he talk -- says that General Ojdanic stuck to his position and after about half an hour he broke off the call. "From the Serb perspective, the build-up of his forces made perfect sense but it could also be a pretext for building up the forces against the Albanians." So these are conversations between General Clark and General Ojdanic that General Clark has made some brief mention of in his book but we feel that the full reports of conversations like this, as well as other information available to General Clark about the chain of command in Kosovo and General Ojdanic's participation would be highly relevant to the issues of the trial and it's a very specific request. Finally, our third request is for information provided by General Ojdanic's predecessor as chief of staff of the Yugoslavian army, General Perisic. And again it's relevant to the same issues; the chain of command and General Ojdanic's participation and knowledge of any plan to expel Albanians from Kosovo. And we cited news articles that General Perisic, after he had left his position as chief of staff, had been arrested for passing classified information to the United States, and we believe that there exists information from General Perisic that is relevant and could -- and necessary to assist us in defending General Ojdanic at the trial. So that's how we've reformulated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, is General Perisic not available to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He is available.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, he's not available to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: First of all, he is an accused here at the Tribunal, and he is also accused of the crime of passing secrets to the Americans in Serbia. So we do not believe that he is in a position to confirm or to provide us with information that he passed to the Americans relating to General Ojdanic. I will tell you I have not specifically asked General Perisic, but I don't believe that he's in a position to be able to do that, and even if he were, I don't think that information he provided would be credible with respect to information that was actually contemporaneously recorded by those who were receiving the information. So we don't believe that there's any prospect of obtaining this information from General Perisic, and even if it were, that it would be as reliable as what we would receive from the States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, though, that you've jumped ahead with that response, because we're not at the stage of assessing the reliability or credibility of any particular account of events. I was thinking more of the identification of the existence of such material, and you haven't even explored with Perisic the possibility that there is available material in the form of reports or comments that he made which you ought to try to recover from the States to which he made it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: To ask General Perisic to confirm the existence of this material, it seems to me, would be asking him to directly incriminate himself for charges that are presently pending against him. I could go through that exercise and do that if the Trial Chamber thought that was important, but I think in my experience, and probably the experience of the Trial Chamber, that is not likely to be a fruitful exercise. Finally, I want to turn to the efforts that we've made to secure the assistance of the States, which is the last component under Rule 54 bis. We've detailed those steps in our application, and the States have also provided evidence of the further steps that were taken since the application was filed. As to the United Kingdom, we accepted their representation that they didn't have any records responsive to items A and B, and we relieved them of providing material in item C(1) because we already obtained from it from the Prosecution. So we're only concerned with items C(2) and C(3) from the United Kingdom, and from our correspondence you can see that we have reached an impasse with respect to voluntary production of that material. As to Canada, they conditioned their voluntary production of material on the use of Rule 70, requiring their consent to use it at trial, and we can't agree to that as we've expressed in the previous hearing. As to the United States, they also conditioned their voluntary participation on the use of Rule 70, but they went a step further and said they would not object to the use of the material they were showing us at the trial. However, they're unwilling to provide all of the material covered by the request, so we've taken the position that we'll look at what they want to show us but it cannot substitute for a Rule 54 bis order. I think our correspondence speaks for itself with respect to our efforts to obtain the material voluntarily from the States, and I'd have to say that, after three years of correspondence, we're yet to receive anything and I think the prospects for a successful voluntary compliance with the request are zero. We've shown our good faith not only in efforts with these States but in accepting the representations of the other States and withdrawing our applications as to them when they've been able to conduct a search of their records and indicate that they have no responsive documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I -- can you clarify what actually you're saying about the United States. I'm not clear about your position. You've taken the position that you'll look at "what they want to show us." Now, you're saying that's historical or is that still the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's still the position. The United States has offered to show us some documents which they've identified as being responsive to our request, and we've accepted that, and the very last thing that was done was we sent them a draft of what we would propose as an order in which we would be allowed to receive those items, but at the same time we acknowledge that this will not result in the withdrawal or satisfaction of our request because the United States is not willing to indicate that all of the materials that will be provided pursuant to this Rule 54 bis request will be done voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was the draft a document drawn up in terms of Rule 70 or --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And when was that sent to them?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: On the 22nd of September. The United States had actually sent us a form that they use for Rule 70 and I adjusted it to reflect their agreement that the materials could be used at the trial if in fact we wanted to use it, and that was the last communication we've had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There seem to be shaking heads behind you but no doubt that will be clarified in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have the correspondence with me, if there is any question about that. Just to conclude and step back from the minutiae of our reformulated request and look at the broader picture, I think we could all agree that there should be no difference between the obligation of the United States, United Kingdom, and Canada to cooperate with the Tribunal and those of other governments such as Serbia and Montenegro. They were on two sides of the same war. And I think we should all agree that there should be no difference between a binding order sought by the Prosecution and a binding order sought by the Defence, because we're on two sides of the same case and have a right to equal access to the process of the Tribunal. So I think you need look no further than your own binding orders that you issued to Serbia and Montenegro at the request of the Prosecution in the Milosevic case, and you allowed the Prosecution to receive all minutes of the Supreme Command of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia for a period of 23 March 1999 to 5 October 2000, which is a period greater than that -- the records we're seeking. And you also allowed the Prosecution to obtain all minutes of the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia and the Council for Harmonisation of Positions on State Policy for the period of April 1990 to June 1997, seven-year period. And if anything, it would seem more important that you don't risk denying evidence to General Ojdanic that could help him establish his innocence, and it would seem also that it's more important to hold these States that created and fund the Tribunal to a high standard of cooperation, even when they don't want to, so we avoid the perception of a victor's justice in this Court. I thank you for your consideration. I hope our efforts to modify and reformulate the request have met with your approval, and I hope that we can move forward towards obtaining the information we need for a fair trial for General Ojdanic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, I'm not sure I like the reference to victor's justice. I don't see how that could be at all applicable to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not saying it's applicable and it's certainly not a criticism of the Tribunal in any way, but I think that it could be perceived that if there was unequal treatment from some States to others and unequal treatment towards the Prosecution against the accused, that a system of victor's justice could be being employed there, but I don't believe that anything has been done to -- to enhance that perception or to validate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The historic significance of that term doesn't have any application in relation to the establishment of this Tribunal, in my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, in relation to call C, you said that you know that documents falling within C exist, but you were no more specific than that and there's nothing in the submission, I don't think, that adds to that assertion. What is it you say you know exists?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honour, that I made that statement with respect to C(2), which is General Clark's reports of General Clark's conversations with General Ojdanic, and I simply believe -- perhaps I used too strong a term of "know," but given the relations of these conversations in his book, it would appear logical that they had been recorded in some official records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So I can read the comment as confined to C(2) and your deduction from what you've read in the book that other more formal records do exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Ms. Swords, on behalf of Canada.

utterances.speaker: MS. SWORDS
utterances.text: Mr. President and members of the Trial Chamber, it's an honour to appear before you again on behalf of the Government of Canada. We had genuinely thought until recently that such a further appearance would be unnecessary. Nevertheless, as the applicant has proceeded with this second Rule 54 bis application at this time, we appreciate the chance to appear before you orally and to suggest some ways for an appropriate and efficient way forward in this matter. In our oral submissions today, we will make two key points. First, this application is premature and unnecessary, which will be demonstrated through a review of our best efforts to voluntarily identify information potentially responsive to elements of the applicant's reformulated request, efforts that have not been made any easier by the approach of the applicant to date. Second, while we do not believe that the order sought by the applicant is necessary or appropriate, today's hearing presents an opportunity to give further direction to the applicant in order to bring the voluntary process to a successful conclusion. I turn first to our most fundamental concern with the applicant's second application, that it is premature and unnecessary and it's a departure from the voluntary procedure ordered by this Chamber in disposing of the first application. In other words, the second application is not a genuine measure of last resort. The mandatory order sought by the applicant is simply not justified. Canada respects its obligations under the Statute and the Rules to act in good faith in responding to requests for assistance, but a party seeking assistance must also act in good faith in accordance with the Statute and the Rules. This means in part that a compulsory order should only be sought when all voluntary avenues of cooperation have been exhausted. This practical and common sense approach is consistent with Article 29 of the Statute of this Tribunal, which is in itself given more detailed expression in Rules 54 and 54 bis. Rule 54 bis (A)(iii) and Rule 54 bis (B)(ii) require that the applicant demonstrate that he has first pursued voluntary measures. And in Blaskic, the Appeals Chamber held that mandatory orders should be sought against States only when they decline to operate voluntarily; that is, only when really necessary. It is for these reasons, we believe, that this Chamber ordered on March 23rd that the applicant pursue the voluntary route with respondents. But pursuing voluntary avenues of cooperation requires more than an unfocused and speculative request followed almost immediately by an application for compulsory measures. Given the complex nature of the interests involved, indeed the potential volume of documents requested, it will often also require more than a single exchange of letters between a requesting party and the requested State. What is required is that the requesting party genuinely and fully exhaust voluntary avenues. He must do so first by making appropriate and reasonable requests that meet the requirements of 54 bis; and second, by agreeing, if asked to do so by a requested State, to apply reasonable protections to information provided by that State, protections that are explicitly contemplated in the Rules of this Tribunal. Failing to do any of these things undermines any real possibility of a successful voluntary process. And that, we submit, has unfortunately been the net effect of the applicant's approach to the voluntary process ordered by this Chamber in March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just be clear about this argument? It seems to me you're saying that because you regard this second request as not complying with the requirements of Rule 54 bis, you should engage in further discussion. Now, if the applicant takes a different view, that he has complied, then it might be said that any continuing debate on that front is simply a waste of time, and that suggests to me that's the real issue, the relevance of the request. And if we were to decide it did satisfy the test, you could hardly complain that he hadn't given you long enough to look through your material; everyone else seems to have been able to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SWORDS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I will come to in my submissions today, we have been able to identify some material in certain cases with respect to his requests, and in other cases we have not. With those things we have been able to identify, we've asked for him to seek a Rule 70 procedure and to follow that, and he has declined to do so since the end of June. So we really have two different categories of issues to present to you today. So what I was just about to do was to explain the status of our search so far and the status of our communications with the applicant, which are evident from the attachments and the annexes to our submission, but I would like to summarise them to make it crystal clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it -- is it fair to say that you haven't really advanced beyond the 24th of June?

utterances.speaker: MS. SWORDS
utterances.text: We have advanced beyond the 24th of June, Your Honour. With respect to paragraph C(1) of his request, we have identified some information that is responsive to that request. We would like to provide that to the applicant under the protections of Rule 70 but we haven't been able to engage in that discussion with the applicant because he has refused to discuss Rule 70 with us. Does that clarify partly the situation? Basically, to summarise where we are, in the spirit of moving forward cooperatively and getting on with the trial, we looked beyond some of the deficiencies that we thought were in the applicant's reformulated request. So, for example, we overlooked the excessive breadth of paragraph A and B of the reformulated request, as well as its focus on a particular method of collection. Through a best-efforts search, some information did turn up that is potentially responsive to the subject matters of paragraph A and B. We offered on June 24th to provide that information to the applicant under the terms of Rule 70. The applicant refused to accept it and has since refused to discuss the matter further with us because his arbitrarily imposed 60-day period for cooperation expired last June. This is all the much harder for us to understand in light of the applicant's recent correspondence with the United States, which we've now seen in the course of this application. That correspondence implies, it seems to us, that the applicant is after all willing to inform -- to receive information from the United States pursuant to Rule 70. The result seems to us to be an unnecessary loss of more than three months in which the applicant could readily have had access to potentially relevant information already identified by Canada. The applicant has tried to justify this rather perfunctory approach by citing an urgent need to prepare for trial. We understand and respect the need for the Tribunal to proceed without delay. However, the applicant's insistence on pursuing a mandatory order is not, in reality, a means of avoiding delay. It has become a cause of it. So in short, the applicant has abandoned, since June 27th, all attempts to resolve the matter voluntarily with Canada, and in our respectful submission that's a clear departure of this Chamber's order of March 23rd. The Chamber ordered that we be given a further opportunity to respond voluntarily, but the applicant, as a somewhat deficient reformulation of his request, he's failed to consider our reasonable proposal that Rule 70 be followed, and he has refused to discuss cooperation since June 27th, and in our submission this amounts to a denial of a genuine opportunity for Canada to respond voluntarily. Achieving results voluntarily is possible, however. In fact, in response to Canada's request for further particulars, the applicant did provide additional information to Canada in his June 24th letter, and this has recently allowed us to identify information responsive to paragraph C(1) of the reformulated request. This too is information that we would willingly share with the applicant in confidence, pursuant to Rule 70. This will allow him to examine it and to determine whether he wishes to make use of it in trial. In other words, the voluntary process can work very well if the applicant is prepared to clarify his requests and to agree to protections that were designed in the Rules to facility state voluntary compliance. This givers the Chamber a snapshot of where our cooperative efforts have led to date. In short, we have identified to the best of our ability, given what we think are some deficiencies under Rule 54 bis in his request, some information that's potentially responsive to the subject matter of paragraph A and B, as opposed to its methods of collection, as well as information responsive to paragraph C(1) of the reformulated request. And we are prepared to provide this information to the applicant in confidence and under the terms of Rule 70. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. There also remains some outstanding difficulties with respect to paragraphs C(2) and C(3) of his reformulated request. With respect to paragraph C(2), the most significant difficulty is that it's simply not clear to us what the applicant is now asking for. Rather than clarifying paragraph C of the original 2002 request, paragraph C(2), as reformulated in April, is entirely new. When we asked for more particulars nevertheless to clarify the scope of this new request, the applicant replied to us in June with a description that actually broadened rather than narrowed the request in C(2). Now, in this application for mandatory measures, the applicant has reverted back to asking for the April version of paragraph C(2). As a purely practical matter, this constantly moving target makes it difficult for Canada to know what information and to search for information that the applicant has asked for when he seems uncertain himself of what he wants. In June and again in August, in correspondence with the applicant, Canada identified other difficulties with paragraph C(2), including the possibility that the information sought might be more readily available from other, more direct sources. However, given the applicant's position that the deadline for voluntary responses was June 27, 2005, our questions have gone unanswered. As a result, we have difficulty in even conceiving of how to go about searching for the information sought in the various versions of C(2). With respect to paragraph C(3), our principal remaining difficulty remains the exceptionally broad nature of the request covering nearly seven years of very vaguely described information which may or may not exist, may or may not be relevant and necessary, and may in any case be more readily available from General Perisic himself. This strikes us as a clear example of an attempt at discovery rather than production of information. With your permission, I would like to move to how we think this hearing can be converted into an opportunity to cut through some of the causes of delay in order to resolve of this matter voluntarily. As indicated above, we continue to believe that cooperation can produce timely and fair results as long as the parties approach it in good faith without arbitrarily imposed deadlines and in accordance with the scheme for voluntary production envisaged in the Rules. What is required is not a mandatory order requiring Canada to respond to a deficient request for information as submitted by the applicant. Canada has already signalled repeatedly its willingness to provide sufficiently identified relevant and necessary information to the applicant. What is needed is for the applicant to bring his request into compliance with 54 bis and to agree to Canada's reasonable proposal that potentially responsive information be provided under the terms of Rule 70. Canada would invite this Chamber to allow the process it had ordered in March to continue by dismissing the second application. In addition, to ensure that the voluntary process bears fruit, Canada also respectfully invites this Chamber to provide the following directions to the applicant: First, the applicant will receive the information which Canada has identified as potentially responsive to the subject matter of paragraphs A, B, and C(1) of his reformulated request in confidence and subject to the provisions of Rule 70. Second, the applicant will demonstrate that it is necessary to seek the information requested in paragraph C(2) and C(3) from Canada rather than from other more direct sources. Assuming he is able to demonstrate this, he will clarify to Canada whether he seeks information as stated in paragraphs C(2) and C(3) of his April reformulated request or, rather, as restated in his June letter to Canada. And third, to the extent he has not already done so, the applicant will provide to Canada the information sought in its letters of June 24th and August 10, 2005. Mr. President, members of the Trial Chamber, Canada would like to take this opportunity to reiterate its commitment to supporting the important work of the Tribunal and to providing appropriate assistance to parties, both Prosecution and Defence, before this Tribunal in the pursuit of international criminal justice. In closing, for all the reasons set out in our written submissions as well as those outlined today, the Government of Canada respectfully requests that this application be dismissed. Subject to any further questions you might have, this concludes Canada's oral submissions on this application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can you clarify for me, then, please, what that additional information is in relation to A and B.

utterances.speaker: MS. SWORDS
utterances.text: I think in this case, Your Honour, it would probably be best if the applicant actually took a look at what we have come up with under A and B. We aren't certain it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no. But you're referring to the suggestion that they should give the information requested in the letters of the -- did you say the 24th of June?

utterances.speaker: MS. SWORDS
utterances.text: The 24th of June and the 10th of August. I believe with respect to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, what is that in relation to A and B? I know what it is in relation to C, but what is it in relation to A and B?

utterances.speaker: MS. SWORDS
utterances.text: Well, with respect to paragraph A and B, we did want to clarify that he's seeking the content of A and B, as opposed to simply one particular method of collection of the content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He could have formulated this request without using the word "intercepted," and by doing it, of course, he set all the States off thinking, "Now how do we protect our national security interests here?" rather than concentrating on what the information is that they actually have. He doesn't want to know anything about your means of acquiring the information, he just wants to know what you've got. And it seems to me the word "intercepted" is unnecessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. SWORDS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. In the previous oral hearing the applicant did indicate that it was the content of the conversations that he was interested in rather than the particular means of collection, and what we've done is search all of our records of all kinds and what we have discovered, and we're not sure it's exactly what he wants. There's not much specificity in it. If he's searching for something in particular, it would help us to have more specificity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's two points there: It's for you to respond to what he asks for rather than, I think, seek more information about what it is he wants; but secondly, if you take away the issue of interception, then does that also not remove the issue of ownership, because the question simply is: Do you have a report on this matter or do you not? If you do, it's yours. And the fact that it may have been the result of an interception by the United States rather than by Canada is again a hare that we don't need to chase.

utterances.speaker: MS. SWORDS
utterances.text: That's an issue perhaps that could be put to the applicant. Canada would certainly not disagree with what Your Honour has just suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But am I right in saying you have given more details about C, but you don't really say specifically that there's anything more you're looking for in relation to B.

utterances.speaker: MS. SWORDS
utterances.text: Well, what we did -- what we did ask in our letter of June 24th with respect to A was if there was specific documents that he was asking for. You will recall he's asking for conversations that took place over a six-month period with 23 different people, and it's -- when you do searches, it's not always possible to key on absolutely everything. We've done what we can, and we're -- we've come up with some things that potentially are relevant. If he believes there is something more specific than that, that's what we're asking for, Your Honour. It's a very broad request and we've done a very broad search. If he has more specificity to give us, we're happy to receive it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Swords. Mr. Raab for the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MR. RAAB
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Again it's an honour to appear before you this afternoon. May I at the outset perhaps just express on behalf of Professor Greenwood and Mr. Whomersley their regrets, because they are unable to attend today because of prior commitments. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber already has the United Kingdom's written submission, which was filed on the 27th of September of this year, and I will not replicate them today. I would rather concentrate on the main points that remain in issue between the applicant and the United Kingdom. There is no dispute about what Rule 54 bis requires. It's been carefully explained in the order of the 23rd of March and in this Tribunal's earlier jurisprudence. An applicant seeking an order that a State produce information must meet four requirements: Firstly, the applicant must show there's been a genuine attempt to obtain the information on a voluntary basis and that the attempt has failed because of the conduct of the State. Secondly, the applicant must be specific regarding what is sought. As the Tribunal has repeatedly made clear, Rule 54 bis is not a mechanism for discovery or the means by which to conduct a fishing expedition. It is the means of obtaining clearly specified information. Thirdly, the applicant must show that the information is relevant to the issues in the case and how it is relevant. And finally, the applicant must show that it is necessary for the Tribunal to issue an order to the State against whom that order is sought. Your Honours, the Chamber's order of the 23rd of March showed that the original request had failed on all four counts, and the Chamber gave the applicant the opportunity to reformulate his request in order to comply with Rule 54 bis, but it did not give him a licence to go away on come back with a wholly new request. And it is an important consideration here because there has to be some finality in a matter which has now dragged on for well over two years. And we submit respectfully, Your Honours, that the revised request contained in the second application, filed on the 27th of June, needs to be evaluated in light of these requests. Your Honours, the revised request still fails to comply with the requirements of Rule 54 bis and the guidance given by this Chamber and elaborated by Judge Bonomy in his separate and concurring opinion, and it fails in four critical respects: First, despite the applicant's attempt to portray the request as a simple refinement of the earlier request, the reality is that a significant part and the whole of what is in issue as between the applicant and the United Kingdom is new. Second, the request still lacks the requisite specificity. This is evident, for example, from paragraph A of the revised request. The applicant is still trying to mount a fishing expedition, requesting production of all recordings, summaries, notes or text of intercepted communications between himself and any of the list of 23 individuals during a period of six months. And although it is the applicant who is best placed to identify what conversations he had, when, with whom, and about what, not a single clue is offered despite the very clear guidance on this particular matter in the order of the 23rd of March and Judge Bonomy's separate opinion of that date. The reality is that the applicant, as he himself has observed today, is still fishing, but contrary to his remarks, is in fact still seeking to drag a very large pond indeed. Thirdly, there is no -- there's still no serious attempt to demonstrate the relevance of important aspects of the request. While the revised request makes some attempt to show what issues parts of the requests might be relevant to, there is still very little attempt to show how they may be relevant to those particular issues. And again, that's in spite of the order of the 23rd of March and the very precise guidance in Judge Bonomy's separate opinion. And fourthly and finally, the applicant persists in trying to obtain an order against the United Kingdom and others for production of material which, if it exists at all, originates from other sources. Your Honours, this particular matter was also raised in argument before the Tribunal in December 2004, although it was not considered in the order of 23rd of March and did not need to be. As counsel for the United Kingdom explained at the December hearing, it cannot be necessary under Rule 54 bis to obtain information from a secondary recipient when the primary source of that material, the originator, is subject to the same obligation. This is especially pertinent where the identity of the originator is clearly known to the applicant. The United Kingdom pointed out all of these problems in its letter to the applicant's counsel of the 24th of June of 2005, annexed at pages 28 to 30 of the second application. In light of that letter, the applicant's counsel Mr. Robinson informed the United Kingdom by letter of the 24th of June, annexed at page 31, that the applicant would not pursue requests A, B and C(1) with regard to the United Kingdom. There was in fact correspondence subsequent to that point in time between the United Kingdom and the applicant. It is not annexed to the second application because that application was filed before the additional correspondence took place and indeed in the lists of ongoing consultations. The UK has therefore attached that correspondence as annexes A, B, and C to its written response. Your Honours, what is striking about this correspondence is that at no point did counsel for the applicant make any attempt to engage with the United Kingdom on the objections about specificity and relevance raised with respect to paragraphs C(2) and C(3). Instead, counsel for the applicant pressed ahead with his application for an order. He then put it on hold while he talked to other States, and then suddenly renewed it. In the United Kingdom's letters to counsel for the applicant of the 24th of June and the 7th of July further details were explicitly sought regarding specificity and relevance of the information under paragraph C. Counsel's reply of the 24th of June failed to address these issues at all. We were therefore somewhat surprised to later learn of counsel's letter to the Government of Canada of the 24th of June, which was attached at pages 25 to 6 of the second application, and the applicant responded as follows, and I'm quoting: "With respect to the three items sought in item C of the request, I'm happy to provide you with more information to assist you locating these materials." Your Honours, the further details provided did not cure the shortcomings of the request but at least demonstrated some effort, however inadequate, to address the shortcomings of the requests for information under paragraph C. However, it appears that counsel for the applicant was not happy to extend even this level of cooperation to the United Kingdom. Your Honours, notwithstanding UK cooperation to date and ongoing efforts to engage seriously and constructively with the applicant, it is clear on the face of the application itself that he has failed to take all reasonable steps to seek voluntary cooperation from the government of the United Kingdom in relation to paragraph C(2) and C(3) of the revised request. The point of Rule 54 bis is that it envisages first and foremost voluntary cooperation. But in his dealings with the United Kingdom, counsel for the applicant has not seriously attempted such cooperation. Instead, he has preferred to hold a sword of Damocles over our heads which he considered he could sheath or brandish at will. Turning to the second application itself, although it makes no formal distinction between the different States to which it is directed, the applicant's letter of the 24th of June makes clear that so far as the UK is concerned, the order sought relates only to paragraph C(2) and C(3), and nevertheless for the avoidance of doubt, I would just like to take the opportunity to reaffirm the points as elaborated in the UK's written response that paragraphs A, B and C(1) of the revised request were misconceived and failed to comply with the requirements of Rule 54 bis. Turning to paragraph C(2), Your Honours, this request is essentially a new request, not a reformulation of the older one. Paragraph C of the original request sought an order for production of: "All correspondence, memoranda, reports, recordings or summaries of any statements made by General Dragoljub Ojdanic during the period 1 January through 20 January, 1999, to any representative of your organisation, including sources of information working on your behalf." Paragraph C(2) of the revised request narrows down the scope of the request by focusing on General Wesley Clark, but introduces two important new elements. Firstly, the time scale is now longer by approximately six months. Secondly, the information sought is no longer confined to statements by the applicant but has been extended to assessments and expressions of opinion about the applicant by General Clark. There has been no attempt to be any more specific about the material sought, despite what we earlier heard of the ostensible knowledge of the applicant of specific documents that exist. Furthermore, there has been no attempt to show how the material sought might be relevant to the issues at trial. In particular, it's difficult to see how General Clark's assessments of the applicant have any bearing on those issues at all. It seems to be more of an attempt to establish something about General Clark than about General Ojdanic. And finally as regards paragraph C(2), Your Honours, General Clark was not a British officer and did not report to the UK. In the language of paragraph C of the original request, General Clark was not a person working for the United Kingdom. It cannot be necessary, as required by Rule 54 bis, to make a binding order against the United Kingdom in respect of information originating from another state in circumstances where the identity of the originator is clearly known to the applicant. Your Honours, turning to paragraph C(3), very similar considerations apply. Firstly, the request is new and extraordinarily broad as to date, extending from November 1998 to the present day, six years after the events to which the indictment relates. It's not limited to information about Kosovo or even the former Yugoslavia. Secondly, it's not suggested that General Perisic worked for or gave material to the United Kingdom. No attempt has been made to specify what conversations took place between General Ojdanic and General Perisic. And there has been no attempt to show how the material sought would be relevant to issues at trial. And as we've already heard earlier, counsel for the applicant has not even attempted to request the information from General Perisic himself. Your Honours, if what is really sought is evidence of something General Ojdanic said to General Perisic, the request needs to be far more specific. On the other hand, if what is sought is evidence of what General Perisic thought of General Ojdanic, and to the extent that it is relevant at all, which we doubt, the appropriate course must be to ask General Perisic. In closing, the United Kingdom respectfully asks the Tribunal to dismiss the application insofar as it concerns the United Kingdom. And unless I can be of further assistance, that concludes my submissions on behalf of the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Raab. Mr. Johnson for the United States of America. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, members of the Court, it is an honour to appear again before this Tribunal on behalf of United States. Nearly a year ago Your Honours heard detailed oral submissions from the United States and other NATO members, objecting to the first application of the accused. That application sought access to highly sensitive intelligence not because the Defence had reason to believe that any of the requested States held specific material that was relevant and necessary to the case but because the Defence hoped that by being given broad access to such intelligence it might discover something of use. The Defence rebuffed various efforts of United States to refocus the request to minimise the national security sensitivity, add specificity, and justify its relevance. Moreover, at the time of the first oral argument, the Defence had rejected for nearly two years an outstanding offer of responsive information from the United States. Your Honours denied the first application but allowed the Defence leave to reformulate it to provide another opportunity to remedy its defects and to pursue voluntary cooperation from the relevant States. What has changed in the intervening year between the first oral hearing and the present one? Regrettably, very little. Despite some superficial changes to parts A and B of the request, it is of the same discovery character as the original. Part C has not been reformulated but, as counsel for the applicant concedes, has been replaced by an altogether new and different request that seeks information beyond the scope of the original. What remains the same with respect to part C is that, like the original, the request is made without any explanation as to its relevance to the issues at trial. As to the process, the Defence has continued its failure to take reasonable steps to obtain the voluntary cooperation of the United States. I will not belabour the history of our dealings with the Defence prior to the first oral hearing, other than to note that they began with a message from the Defence indicating an expectation, indeed a desire, to bring this matter to litigation, and they have continued in that vein to date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Johnson, you're not the first to suggest that there hasn't been an attempt to explain the relevance of these matters to issues in the trial, but surely the four issues which are set out in subparagraph (3) of both A and B, and they're also incorporated into C, are clearly issues that you can identify as issues at the trial and the state of mind which can often be determined from what is said by a person as well as what he does is surely something that's relevant to each of these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do think they help focus the request and in a little bit in my submission I will analyse that issue in particular. And if any question remains, I will try to respond again, Your Honour. Just as the United States' efforts to work with the Defence cooperatively to narrow the focus of the first request and minimise its security sensitivity were rebuffed our similar efforts to engage the Defence on the revised request were also rejected. Our interactions since the first hearing are detailed in the submission we filed last week but I would just highlight a recent example for you. On August 25th, 2005, at the Status Conference Your Honours held with respect to the request, the Defence agreed that it was premature to proceed with an application for a 54 bis order because it was engaged with discussions with two States, presumably including the United States. On August 29, four days later, and over two and a half years after having first been offered certain responsive information by the United States, the Defence finally accepted our offer to receive it subject to the same conditions to protect the information we had requested originally. But despite the representation at the Status Conference and while we were working out the modalities to provide this information - and I would just note in this respect that the letter counsel referred to of September 22nd was -- we simply never received that by e-mail or fax or hard copy - the Defence without notice to us changed tacks and informed the Chamber on September 6th - this is just a week after it accepted our offer - that it was necessary to bring this matter to judicial decision. In a footnote to its Status Conference report, the Defence apologised "for taking a more deliberative position at the Status Conference," but when dealing with States on a request like the present one, a more deliberative position is precisely what I would submit is called for. Working cooperatively with States to refine and focus a request and address their concerns, as my colleagues have outlined, is an essential aspect of the obligation to take reasonable steps to obtain voluntary cooperation. The Defence has failed to do this, and the present application should be rejected on that ground alone. But beyond the failure to cooperate, the request itself remains fundamentally deficient and falls far short of the threshold required by Rule 54 bis and the Tribunal's jurisprudence. In the remainder of my presentation, I intend to address each part of the revised request against the guidelines Your Honours laid out in your decision of March 23rd. I hope to show that parts A and B of the request continue to lack the requisite specificity, and more significantly, fail to establish relevance. I will also show that irrespective of whether you find the necessary specificity and relevance, that portion of the request is moot and should be dismissed because United States has already answered it. We informed the Defence on June 20, 2005, that we had reviewed all information in our possession within the scope of the request to ensure that the United States had no exculpatory information relevant to any of the four issues referred to by Judge Bonomy and identified by the Defence as being relevant to the case. We found no such information. All that remains of this request, therefore, is that portion of it which was over-broad and irrelevant to begin with; namely, information that is not within the potentially exculpatory categories identified by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why do you -- why do you say, both in your written submission and today, that this request is confined to exculpatory material?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: Well, my submission, Your Honour, is that the request itself is overly broad because, with respect to those four categories, it encompasses information that would be potentially exculpatory as well as information that is not. And our submission is that, to the extent the Defence is asking the information relevant to the Defence case, would presumably be that which would tend to mitigate the guilt of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you see, that then means that you arrogate to yourself the right to determine what is and what is not exculpatory, and surely that's not the job of any State from whom material is sought. Surely the simple job of the State is to try to identify material which is covered by a request.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, my response to that is that we are being placed in that position by the nature of an overly broad Defence request to begin with. If the request itself had been more specific and had identified and focused on specific content, then our government would have been in a better position to respond precisely to those bits of information asked for. The Defence, despite our repeated requests, has been unable to do so, and that puts us in the position of either rejecting it wholesale as an inadequate request, or making the effort we have to try to move this process forward of distilling from that those portions that would seem to be relevant and pertinent to the case. I guess the other point I would add is that in the Rule 68 context, when you are dealing with parties directly opposed to each other, the Prosecution and the Defence, the Prosecution is entrusted in that context with doing precisely what you stated, making a judgement about its holdings and whether it has information that is potentially exculpatory that must be disclosed. So I would submit that when dealing with a third party State that is not directly involved in an adverse proceeding with a party, it isn't so incongruous for us to take that approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Johnson, if you could elaborate on the issue why you say the request A(1) is too over broad.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will get to that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will wait for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: With your permission, I will get to that. I'm concerned if I try to jump the gun, I'll end up confusing matters more than being clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: To finish my -- to finish my initial overview, I would just note that, as for part C, this request is new, as the Defence has conceded, and no effort has been made by the Defence to respond to the United States' queries and explain its relevance, justify its necessity, or explain why the United States is in the best position to provide the requested information. And I would note, as my UK colleague did, that it wasn't until we saw the Canadian submission of the September 28 and the annexed letters that we realised the Defence had in fact engaged in some back-and-forth with Canada with respect to C. That kind of response never occurred in our communication. The failures of the Defence to meet the required standards with respect to all three parts of the request would be enough on their own to warrant dismissal but become all the more significant given the serious national security implications of the request. As we have previously explained, the request as framed is directed at information of the highest national security sensitivity, and at a minimum, this should reinforce the need to hold it to the highest standards of meeting the requisite requirements. Now, let me move, as Your Honours have indicated, to a more detailed review of parts A and B of the revised request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I need to be clear on this. You can't tell whether the information is of the highest national security sensitivity, can you? And --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: What I would -- what I submit, Your Honour, is that had the request not been phrased, as you have suggested on a number of occasions, to focus on intercepted communications, then this issue would not present itself so directly. But despite the previous argument we had on this issue, despite the suggestions of Your Honour, the second application retained that precise language, and as long as that precise language remains there, a response by us confined to that request would seem to directly implicate these kinds of sensitive national security issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Johnson, it doesn't seem to me that's the way you go about your negotiations. You go about your negotiations, it would appear, on the basis that we will see if there is any material and we'll discuss with you, if you're willing to engage, whether we might provide that material on a certain basis. You don't get into the question of how you got the material, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: In terms of our dealings with the Defence, you're precisely right, Your Honour, that we try to -- request on the face of it was one that raised these serious concerns and went back to the Defence with suggested ways to rephrase that in a way that would not present these. And in fact, the outstanding request of information that has been outstanding for nearly three years was in response to a reformulation of the original request that had deleted the reference to intercepted communications, but then as that proceeded, that language came back in. But I accept what you are saying, Your Honour, that to the extent the request is not focused on that, we have endeavoured in our dealings with the Defence to change that focus --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, if we make an order to produce material and then you discover something that the production of would lead to some impact on your national security interests, then you can ask us thereafter to do something about that. And equally, you can not only use Rule 70 now, but it would appear, from what the Appeals Chamber has recently decided, that you can actually voluntarily provide information and then seek, at the same -- or agree to, and then seek protective measures for that material. So whether national security interests are affected is a matter we can look at later, is it not? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: I do think it is an issue that arises later, and I would say, particularly given our position, that we have responded with respect to parts A and B of the request, which I think present the most acute issues in terms of national security, and I would certainly associate myself with the argument made by my colleague from Canada, but one needs to approach this looking not just at Rule 54 but at the other relevant Rules, including Rule 70. It would seem anomalous to us in a Rule 70 context in dealing with the Prosecution we could protect precisely this kind of national security information, but with the Defence, that could be leapfrogged over. And we would take the same view that our colleague from Canada does about the necessity of the use of Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think there is a difference. The Prosecution just happen to accept material from you under Rule 70 but they could just easily refuse to accept it and apply under Rule 54. It just happens to be the case they don't intend to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we're talking about a theoretical issue, Your Honour, but we would take perhaps a different view of how that issue might turn out. With respect to the parts of requests A and B, I will not -- I will briefly summarise what they are because I think it is relevant to how the United States construed and applied them. Part A seeks copies of intercepted communications that took place during an approximately six-month period between the accused and any one of 23 named interlocutors that he participated in from Belgrade, although as I understand from their earlier submission, since he was in Belgrade the whole time, this is hardly a restriction. And that, quote "may be relevant to one of four issues; the first knowledge or participation in the deportation of Albanians from Kosovo or lack thereof; second, knowledge or participation in the killing of civilians in Kosovo or lack thereof; whether a formal chain of command on matters pertaining to Kosovo was respected within the FRY or Serbian governments; and lastly, efforts to prevent and punish war crimes in Kosovo or lack thereof." Part B of the revised request seeks copies of any intercepted communication in which the accused was mentioned took place during the same time period and took place at least partly in the FRY involving at least one party who held a position in the government, armed forces, or police and that may be relevant to one of the same four issues enumerated with respect to A. Now, our pre-hearing submission details how parts A and B of the revised request continue to fail to meet the requirements of 54 bis with respect to specificity, relevance and necessity, but what I would like to focus on now is how they fail to meet the standards that Your Honours laid out with respect to the first application. In your March 23rd decision, you stated that a requesting party must "identify as far as possible the documents and information to which the application relates" and must "identify specific documents and not broad categories." Your Honours also noted that part A of the request did not attempt to state when and where the communications took place and did not mention the issues the communications might relate to. With respect to B, you observed that it did not identify the issues to which the documents sought relate. Your Honours further suggested that in order to reformulate parts A and B appropriately, the Defence should also specify "as far as possible, the place and dates of the intercepted communications sought." And Your Honour Judge Bonomy provided further elaboration in this direction, observing that the accused is particularly well placed to make an application for relevant material with respect to part A which seeks information regarding statements made by him and that "he will certainly be able to set out the places, such as an office, where and the sorts of occasions on which he probably had telephone discussions relating to matters which are the subject of the indictment. He is also obliged to specifically identify the matters in issue in the case to which the documents he seeks are said by him to be relevant and to indicate how they're relevant to these matters." In our submission, all of these directives are consistent with a fundamental principle of Rule 54 bis; namely, that it is a tool used to obtain specific relevant and necessary information that an applicant has reason to believe exists and not a means to conduct discovery on governments in the hope of finding something useful. If the Defence is aware of specific relevant conversations about which it seeks information, then it should not be difficult for it to provide the details urged by Your Honours, such as the place, date, participants, and content of the specific conversation sought. But the Defence has done no such thing in its revised request because, despite various minor changes, it remains in essence an attempt at discovery. The Defence doesn't refer to specific conversations it is seeking information about because it isn't seeking information about specific conversations. It is instead trying to capture a broad sweep of conversations in a six-month period involving any of 23 participants in the hope that one of them may have useful content. What that content is we don't know because the defendant remains unable to attach specific content to a specific conversation. Indeed, the Defence has not even been able to allege that the conversations are exculpatory. Its request also encompasses, as I discussed before, conversations that show the accused's knowledge or participation in the alleged crimes. In our submission, a properly formulated request would be premised on the content of the information sought. It would describe the content of the alleged conversation and the participants and provide information as to its approximate date. Of the thousands of conversations that are potentially swept up within the scope of the revised request, the Defence has been unable to do this with respect to even one conversation. It is for similar reasons that the revised request continues to fail to meet the relevance requirement. Your Honours stated that under Rule 54 bis and the Tribunal's jurisprudence, the requesting party must indicate how the document or -- the documents or information to which the application relates are relevant to any matter at issue in the case, and "necessary for a fair determination of that matter." While the addition of the four "issues in the case" to which the conversations "may be relevant" provides a clear indication of what the Defence is hoping to find in its discovery mission, it does nothing to describe how a particular conversation sought is relevant to the case. The Defence has described theoretical relevance, not actual relevance. In other words, the Defence is saying that if a conversation record is found that touches on one of these issues, then it is relevant. But we would submit that that puts the whole process backwards. The request needs to proceed from an assertion that in a specific conversation the accused made a statement touching on specific relevant matters in the case. If that was the case, then the relevance of the conversations or their lack thereof could be readily established, but the Defence cannot do this and does not do it because to date it has not alleged any such specific conversations that it is seeking to corroborate. But even if Your Honours were satisfied that the revised request met the specificity and relevance requirements of 54 bis, we would submit that it should be dismissed with prejudice because it has been answered in relevant part by the United States and no amount of reformulation will change that answer. In an effort to be responsive both to the Defence and to efforts of this Chamber to bring this protracted saga to a close, the United States took the initiative to apply a reasonable construction to the request and conduct a search for relevant material. The premise of the United States' effort was the directive of Your Honours to the accused as detailed by Judge Bonomy which was "to start by identifying the issues in the case to which the material is relevant." We therefore began with the four issues delineated by the Defence as being of potential relevance to the case. As I noted previously, the Defence described two of the relevant issues as going to the accused's knowledge or participation in the deportation or killings or the lack thereof. We focused on the lack thereof because only such information would be germane to the Defence. The Defence also described a third relevant issue as being the accused's efforts to "prevent and punish war crimes" or lack thereof. In this case we focused on the efforts and not the "lack thereof" because only the former would be relevant to the Defence. The final relevant issue described by the Defence was whether the formal chain of command was respected. Again, since only information indicating that it was respected would be relevant to the Defence case, we focused on that aspect. We then conducted a search of all information in the possession of the United States that was within the scope of the request and relevant to it the issues as construed -- as I just described. That search did not exclude any types or categories of information. That search turned up no, no responsive information and we reported that in writing to the Defence on June 20, 2005. As I would hope is clear from my description, the only information that was not captured in the scope of our search was information outside the scope of the request or that was either not relevant or incriminating. Such information, by definition, cannot be relevant or necessary to the Defence case. Therefore, because our search and response encompassed the relevant matters in parts A and B of the Defence request, those parts of the request should be dismissed with no any opportunity for reformulation, at least with respect to the United States. Let me now turn to part C of the revised request. As originally formulated, the request in part C asked for records of any statements made by General Ojdanic during the period 1 January through 20 June 1999 to any representative of the United States. In the Trial Chamber's March decision on the first application, you rejected the original request because the applicant "had failed to identify as far as possible the documents sought," and had failed "to indicate how they are relevant and necessary." And Judge Bonomy, you elaborated on this conclusion and explained that the principal difficulty with respect to part C was that the applicant had advanced only a "general, vague and obscure description of the material sought" and that the request lacked basic clarity. Part C of the request has been reformulated in the new application but, rather than clarifying the original request, it is -- the applicant has essentially advanced several new requests, as he conceded. All three requests are outside the time frame of the original request in the indictment, and C(2) and C(3) seek for the first time information relating to Generals Perisic and Clark rather than statements of the accused, which was the focus of the original. We did not consider as a preliminary matter that these new requests are appropriate under the Chamber's order of March 23rd which gave the Defence leave to reformulate the original requests rather than leave to file new requests. But leaving aside the issue of newness of part C, it is clear that these requests also fail to meet the requirements of 54 bis. While C(1) and, to a lesser degree, C(2) and C(3) are more specific than the original, they fail completely to make any showing as to how they are relevant and necessary. The Defence does not allege the purported content of any of the information targeted in C or explain how third party assessments about the accused are relevant to whether or not he committed the crimes at issue. For example, in C(1), the applicant seeks others' reactions to a speech that he admittedly gave and which we learnt today he apparently also has a copy of. He claims that this is needed to prove what was actually said in the speech and to counter testimony given by Colonel Crosland in the Milosevic trial. The accused has not, however, explained how the speech, let alone its characterisation by third parties, is relevant or necessary to the Defence in this case. Moreover, if he gave the speech and has a copy, he would be best positioned to know what was in it and to make assertions about that. Part C(2) suffers from similar flaws. This is a very broad request seeking general opinions of General Wesley Clark on General Ojdanic.
