It is not clear how the subjective opinions of General Clark on the accused's "attitude, position and competence" could be relevant to the Defence in this case or how they would be necessary to a fair determination of the matters at issue. Part C(3), which seeks information allegedly provided by General Perisic, likewise lacks a showing of relevance or necessity. As with parts A and B of the request, it also fails to specify the particular content sought. It is instead a broad request for any information General Perisic may have provided in the hope that there is something useful in it for the Defence. And as others have stated before me, it is unclear why the Defence would seek this information from States rather than seeking it directly from General Perisic. Not only has the Defence failed to demonstrate sufficient relevance and necessity with respect to these part C requests, but it has also failed to take reasonable steps to obtain this information from the United States. The April 2005 formulation of part C is essentially a series of new requests and the Defence has jumped into litigation with respect to these requests rather than engage in a good faith effort to seek the information on a voluntary basis from the United States. Our letter of June 20, 2005, detailed our concerns about the absence of a showing of relevance and necessity with respect to part C of the request and offered assistance to develop a further request that addressed the concerns raised. The Defence never responded to this offer or sought to address these issues. Instead, its reply and subsequent exchanges of correspondence with us focused exclusively on the information we had offered to make available to the Defence in January 2003. And as I noted, it was not until we saw Canada's filing of September 27th that we realised that the Defence had in fact engaged in such an exchange with that government. Because the Defence has failed to take reasonable steps to obtain the cooperation of the United States with respect to this new request, and because it failed to establish its relevance and necessity of the material sought, we submit that part C of the request should be dismissed. Before I conclude my oral presentation, I would like to reiterate the serious national security implications of the request as currently framed and how they are relevant to your consideration of the application. As we have stated before, the United States has a compelling national security interest in protecting information about intelligence sources and methods, including whether or not we possess particular intelligence information. Disclosure of such information may reveal the extent and nature of United States' capabilities and where and how they might be directed. A state's ability to protect its sources and methods, including not to reveal their existence, scope and use, is fundamental to their effectiveness, and when such information is released, it compromises not just the information gathered through the source or method but the source or method itself. These are -- such information is among the most highly protected of national security assets and goes to the heart of state sovereignty and security. The fact that the present request implicates national security information of high sensitivity requires, if not the outright denial of such a request, at a minimum that any effort to compel its production and thereby intrude into aspects of the state sovereignty be held to the highest standards and subjected to rigorous scrutiny. The Blaskic Court contemplated such an intrusion in cases where the information sought by the Tribunal might be "of decisive importance" or "crucial." We would submit that the present request does not approach such a standard. Moreover, the Tribunal recognised the importance of this issue when it established Rule 70 to provide a mechanism for providers to share sensitive information without compromising their sources or methods, and to allow a defendant to have resource to Rule 54 bis without engaging in a Rule 70 process with a provider would, we would submit, vitiate this protection. To conclude: Parts A and B of the revised request retain the fundamental flaws of the original. They seek access to a broad category of information in the hope of discovering something relevant rather than seeking specific information that the Defence knows to be relevant. The Defence has failed to establish the specificity, relevance, and necessity of the request. And moreover, A and B should be dismissed with prejudice because the United States has conducted a search that addressed all relevant aspects of the request and located no responsive material. Part C of the request is essentially three new requests. The Defence has not established the relevance and necessity of the information sought nor has the Defence with respect to any parts of that revised request engaged in a genuine effort to work with the United States to address our concerns and obtain information voluntarily. For all of these reasons, as well as those detailed in our written submissions, we request that the second application be rejected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Johnson, could you clarify one thing about Rule 70 for me. If a party accepts material under Rule 70, how does he then make use of the material or get authority to use it should it turn out to be valuable in his eyes for the presentation of his case?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've had a fair amount of experience in that respect, and the practice that we have followed with both the Prosecution and with the Defence, we apply equal standards to both, is that when information is shared under Rule 70, if they believe any of it is relevant for use at trial, they come to us with a request, they explain and justify why they believe it is -- it is necessary, and then we -- we respond. And if we provide authorisation, then that material is used. I can tell Your Honours that in every case involving both the Prosecution and the Defence that we have received such requests, we have provided the authorisation. We may request that specific protective measures be added to govern the use and modalities of it, but that has been our practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's assume just for the moment that you don't agree. Are the hands of the applicant then tied because, rather than using Rule 54, he went down the Rule 70 road with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: In that case we would submit that they would be, because if they weren't, then there would be no purpose, frankly, to Rule 70 because any party could then skip over it and go to Rule 54 bis if they didn't like the answer they received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That would explain the reluctance of any Defence counsel to go down the route of Rule 70, would it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can understand that, but I think that's also a decision the Tribunal made when it put Rule 70 into place. It recognised that there needed to be a trade-off and that Rule 70 allowed governments a mechanism to share sensitive information that otherwise might not be shared with the Tribunal, and the trade-off of this was to provide some assurance to the governments about how that information was used and protected. We would submit that was the purpose of it, and if Rule 54 bis is allowed to essentially trump it, then information that has been shared under Rule 70 with an expectation of its being protected would suddenly become, after it has been shared, stripped away of that protection under 54 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson made a point which was picked up earlier, that it is difficult to accept that an organisation comprising a number of States can go to war with another State, that that State's serving soldiers should then be the subject of a criminal proceedings, and the countries that went to war with them then say, oh, well we're not handing over the material that you seek because we have national security interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I mean, first I would point out the United States nor any of these other States are involved in these particular proceedings, and unlike other States that the Prosecution and others have dealt with in the region, our approach and that of other NATO governments, we would submit, has been consistently to cooperate with the Tribunal and with requests from both the Defence and Prosecution. There isn't an absence of good faith in that respect. There is not a record of my government, or I would submit, any of these others, abusing the protections offered by the Tribunal and not responding to legitimate requests. And as has been reflected in some of the decisions of this Tribunal, there is a basis to view governments such as ours in a different stead from those that have been resistant to and, frankly, have on occasion obfuscated efforts by the Tribunal to proceed. The other point I would emphasise, Your Honour, is that we are -- we are sensitive to that concern and that is why our consistent practice has been to find ways and to work with counsel, both on the Defence and the Prosecution, to make relevant information available, and we have been very successful in that respect with the exception of this case before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand the point particularly in relation to C(3) where it actually takes you up-to-date, but in relation to the rest of it, it's largely historical. And I certainly for one, speaking for myself, can see the reason for reluctance on the part of any Defence counsel in not going down the Rule 70 route.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: I would submit, Your Honour, that that's a decision for Defence counsel to make in a particular case, but that if they decide not to go down that route, the alternative shouldn't be to compel the governments to expose sensitive information that otherwise under Rule 70 could be protected, because again that would make Rule 70 purposeless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me ask one question before we break. Let me go back to the issue of specificity. You said several times that materials should be specifically relevant. So I'm of the impression that you, by using the term "specific relevance," are trying to combine two requirements, specificity and relevance, together, thereby making the requirements more restrictive. Speaking for myself, I take specificity as being identifiable, as was -- as is provided by Rule 54 bis (A)(i). So the Chamber, as well as the separate and concurring opinion of Judge Bonomy, didn't raise the issue of -- I'm sorry, I beg your pardon, the issue of specificity in relation to request A(1). So what mattered was relevance. But the Rule doesn't say it should be specifically relevant or whether it should be exculpatory or not. So I don't think it is for the State to assess the material to be specifically relevant or exculpatory. Of course it is a separate matter if that job is too onerous or overly burdensome for the State. It's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOHNSON
utterances.text: Judge Kwon, I take your point, and I may misrecollecting this, but it may be in Judge Bonomy's concurring opinion he spoke of the different requirements being to some degree intertwined. Or at least, that's in one of the Tribunal's decisions. And I think to some extent that that is true. So it may that be some of these arguments are being made with respect to one word are better attached to another but I don't think that the net effect is to create a higher standard than is otherwise required by the Rule. Our principal concern with a lot of this reformulated request, and particularly A and B, is that it does not proceed from seeking specific content, a specific conversation, something like that, where, if that were shown, it would be easy for Your Honours and anybody else to assess whether it was relevant or not. Instead, what's happening is a broad basket of information is being sought and there is an element of it being onerous to searching for thousands of -- potentially thousands of conversations and then the idea is to sift through those and maybe one of those is relevant to the four issues identified in the request. We don't think that that's -- we think that puts the process under 54 backwards. And it's because the Defence has done that that we feel we are in a -- that we feel are we are in a position where we are confronted with a request that is overly broad and that does not have the necessary specificity attached to the content. There is no assertion of specific content here. If that was the case, then the United States would not be in the position that you have suggested, of making some assessment as to whether something is exculpatory or not. We could look for records of a particular conversation and, if those existed, an assertion was made as to why it was relevant, we would be in a position to provide that or to explain why we would not provide it. But that's not what we're confronted with here, and it's because we are confronted with something different where that type of specificity and relevance has not been made with respect to the specific content, that we constructed, we construed the request as we did in an effort to move this process forward. And again, we didn't do it making up our own categories of what's exculpatory or not. We took the categories as described by the Defence itself and, as with any search, it's up to the requested party to conduct that search, so we don't feel that involved any more of a judgement by us in focussing on that aspect than otherwise. I'm not sure if that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Johnson. Mr. Robinson, if you can give your concluding remarks in ten minutes, then we can go on without breaking. I understand, for technical reasons, we would have to break in ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I can do that, Mr. President. That's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I thought you would be able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't need to keep you longer than necessary. Well, the first thing about Rule 70 and Rule 54 bis, I think, is a very important issue before this Tribunal and one that hasn't been addressed directly in the jurisprudence: Can a party be compelled to go through Rule 70 instead of Rule 54 bis? And I would simply point out, as Judge Bonomy has, the reasons why we do not feel we can be compelled. And it's just a question of control. We want the Trial Chamber to control the decisions about whether evidence can be used or not rather than the State against whom -- who went to war against General Ojdanic. And that's as simple as that. If the Trial Chamber has that control, we're happy. And you can use Rule 54 bis (G), (F), (I) to exercise the control in a way that's very consistent with the national security interests of the State, and that Rule 54 bis provides for that. So we don't think we can be compelled to use Rule 70 and we don't want to use Rule 70 because it will leave the control in the hands of the United States or another State. Going to Judge Bonomy's question about intercepted conversations and can we exclude the word 'intercepted.' If we did that, we would broaden considerably the communications that would be subject to this request. We would have media reports of General Ojdanic's public statements would be communications from General Ojdanic during this period. We could have speeches made by General Ojdanic that were reported by the attaches or the other people who were inside Yugoslavia at the time, so it would broaden rather than narrow the request to take out the word "intercepted." Secondly, what would we get in terms of the result? What's important and what makes the evidence of an intercepted conversation particularly probative is the fact that it came from an interception, that it was an unguarded conversation between General Ojdanic and some other person at a time contemporaneous with the events, not some piece of paper that comes into evidence with no foundation as to where it came from or how it was obtained that says that General Ojdanic on some occasion said something. So the fact that it's an intercepted conversation is part of the foundation for which we would seek to use and admit the evidence and it's a necessary and reliable aspect to the fact finding process that would go on at the trial. The government doesn't want to confirm or deny that it intercepts conversations, yet at the hearing in December I played for you General Powell's comments to the United Nations while the whole world was watching in which he played an intercepted conversation between Iraqi soldiers that had been intercepted just one week before his speech. So it's not very convincing that the United States doesn't want to confirm or deny that it intercepts conversations when it's being requested for use in a criminal trial and they're happy to do it when it's being used to convince people that they should go to war in Iraq. Now, turning to the United Kingdom's point that there was -- that this is a new request. Again, I don't think that should make any difference. We've narrowed the request. We've tried. If it's considered new, we're entitled to make a new request. So I believe that it doesn't really advance anything to say whether this is a new request or not. It's now before the Trial Chamber. We're entitled to bring that and we did it and with the goal of narrowing the issues in this request as opposed to broadening them, and I think we've been successful to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It has no substantive implications whether it's new or not. It's just a procedural matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. With respect to the United Kingdom's objections with respect to specificity and relevance as to paragraph A, it's incongruous because at the same time they went and searched and they've represented to us that they made a thorough search and were unable to find any items responsive to the request, and so obviously it was specific enough for them to do that, which is the point of the specificity requirement. They say that material originating from other sources shouldn't be -- they shouldn't be compelled to produce items in its possession that came from other sources. And it may very well be that if we obtain the information from other sources, we don't have to ask the United Kingdom to provide it. But I don't know if you're aware of the letter that was filed by NATO today, but we received something on our e-mail before we came to Court, a letter from NATO saying that they don't have General Clark's material that we've asked for in item C(2), and they in general object to our request. And so if NATO doesn't have item C(2), then perhaps they share or they disperse their information to the other States and perhaps the United Kingdom may be one of the originating sources or the only sources from which we could get this information. And there's no authority that I know of that says that if -- when you ask for an order or subpoena for something in someone's possession they're not excused from providing it simply because it's also in someone else's possession. I don't think there's any law that I've seen on that. Finally, with respect to the question of content and Mr. Johnson's point that you should look to the content, that somehow we're required to provide the content of every conversation before we're entitled to seek evidence of intercepted conversations, I would point out that when you allowed the Prosecutor to get the minutes of the Supreme Command of Yugoslavia, or when you allowed them to get the minutes of the Assemblies, you didn't require them to specify the content of any particular meetings over that seven-year or one-year period because the nature of the -- of the evidence itself showed you that it was relevant and it was specific enough that the government of Serbia and Montenegro could find it. The same thing is here. Intercepted conversations of General Ojdanic's contemporaneous conversations about the four issues that we've laid out is clearly relevant and it's specific enough that they could find it. That's all that's needed, and I think that if you look at it that way, then our request should be granted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Robinson, and I thank all the parties for their submissions, and the Trial Chamber will give a decision shortly. We are adjourned.
